questions.stem: Which behaviour is a result of maturation rather than learning?
questions.explanation: Maturation is development that unfolds according to a genetic timetable, such as walking, which appears when the body and nervous system are ready. Bike riding, sitting on command and texting are learned.

questions.stem: Every bird of a particular species builds the same type of nest, even when raised alone without ever seeing a nest. This is:
questions.explanation: A fixed action pattern is a complex, unlearned sequence of behaviour shown by all members of a species in response to a particular trigger. A reflex is a simpler, automatic response to a stimulus.

questions.stem: In Pavlov's experiments, before conditioning, the bell was a:
questions.explanation: Before conditioning, the bell produced no salivation, so it was a neutral stimulus. After repeated pairing with food it became a conditioned stimulus.

questions.stem: Each time a family opens a tin of cat food, they use an electric can opener. Soon the cat runs to the kitchen at the sound of the opener. The conditioned stimulus is:
options: the cat food in the tin
the sound of the can opener
questions.explanation: The sound was initially neutral and, through repeated pairing with food (the unconditioned stimulus), now produces the response on its own, making it the conditioned stimulus.

questions.stem: A dog conditioned to salivate to a high-pitched tone also salivates, a little less, to a slightly lower tone. This is:
questions.explanation: Stimulus generalisation is responding to stimuli similar to the conditioned stimulus. The more similar the stimulus, the stronger the response.

questions.stem: After conditioning, a bell is repeatedly rung without food and the dog gradually stops salivating. A day later, the bell is rung and the dog salivates again. This return is:
questions.explanation: Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of an extinguished conditioned response after a rest period. It shows extinction does not erase the learning.

questions.stem: In Watson and Rayner's (1920) 'Little Albert' study, a loud noise was made each time Albert touched a white rat. What were the unconditioned stimulus and the conditioned response?
options: UCS: the loud noise; CR: fear of the noise
UCS: the white rat; CR: fear of the rat
UCS: the loud noise; CR: fear of the rat
UCS: the white rat; CR: fear of the noise
questions.explanation: The loud noise naturally produced fear (UCS producing UCR). After pairing, the rat (now the CS) produced fear on its own, which is the conditioned response.

questions.stem: Albert later showed fear of a rabbit and a fur coat. Which ethical problem is most serious in Watson and Rayner's study?
options: Albert was told the true aim of the study before it began
Albert's mother gave permission for him to take part in the study
Albert's responses were recorded on film by the researchers
Albert was caused distress and his fear was never removed
questions.explanation: The study deliberately caused fear in an infant, and there is no record of the conditioned fear being extinguished before he left. This would not be approved by an ethics committee today.

questions.stem: A person becomes ill after eating oysters once and afterwards feels nauseous at the sight of them. Why is this called one-trial learning?
options: The person watched someone else become ill one time
The response was learned through repeated practice
A conditioned response formed after a single pairing
The person was punished once for eating the oysters
questions.explanation: Taste aversions often form after only one pairing of a food with illness, unlike most classical conditioning, which needs repeated pairings.

questions.stem: A therapist teaches a client with a fear of dogs to relax, then gradually exposes them to a list of feared situations, from a photo of a dog to patting one. This is:
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitisation combines relaxation training with gradual exposure to a fear hierarchy, so relaxation replaces fear as the response. Flooding uses intense exposure from the start.

questions.stem: A client with a fear of lifts is taken into a lift and stays there, with support, until the fear subsides. This is:
questions.explanation: Flooding involves immediate, prolonged exposure to the feared stimulus without escape, until the anxiety response is extinguished. It is quick but can be distressing.

questions.stem: In aversion therapy, a person who wants to stop biting their nails paints them with a bitter-tasting liquid. In classical conditioning terms, what happens?
options: Nail biting becomes linked with an unpleasant taste, producing aversion
Nail biting is rewarded each time it occurs, so the habit grows stronger
The person watches others stop nail biting and copies their behaviour
The person is exposed to nail biting until the fear of it disappears
questions.explanation: Aversion therapy pairs an unwanted behaviour with an unpleasant stimulus, so the behaviour comes to produce a negative response. The bitter taste is the UCS and the cue of nail biting becomes the CS.

questions.stem: Skinner's three-phase model of operant conditioning consists of:
questions.explanation: In the three-phase (ABC) model, the antecedent is the stimulus that signals a behaviour may be reinforced, the behaviour is the response, and the consequence affects whether it is repeated.

questions.stem: A student puts on a seatbelt to stop the car's warning beep. Putting on the seatbelt is strengthened by:
questions.explanation: Negative reinforcement strengthens a behaviour by removing an unpleasant stimulus, here the beep. It is reinforcement, not punishment, because the behaviour becomes more likely.

questions.stem: A teenager loses phone privileges for a week after coming home late. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Response cost removes a desirable stimulus to make a behaviour less likely, so it is a form of punishment. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant to make a behaviour more likely.

questions.stem: Which statement about punishment and negative reinforcement is correct?
options: Punishment weakens a behaviour; negative reinforcement strengthens it
Punishment strengthens a behaviour; negative reinforcement weakens it
Both weaken a behaviour by adding an unpleasant stimulus after it
Both strengthen a behaviour by removing a pleasant stimulus after it
questions.explanation: Reinforcement, positive or negative, always makes a behaviour more likely. Punishment makes it less likely. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant, whereas punishment adds something unpleasant or removes something pleasant.

questions.stem: Money is called a secondary reinforcer because:
options: it is given after a set number of responses have been completed
it removes an unpleasant stimulus after the behaviour is shown
its value is learned through association with primary reinforcers
it satisfies a biological need such as hunger or thirst directly
questions.explanation: Secondary (conditioned) reinforcers gain value through association with primary reinforcers such as food and warmth. Primary reinforcers satisfy biological needs without learning.

questions.stem: A salesperson is paid a bonus for every ten phones she sells. Which schedule of reinforcement is this?
questions.explanation: A fixed-ratio schedule reinforces after a set number of responses. A variable ratio reinforces after an unpredictable number, as with poker machines.

questions.stem: Poker machine players often keep playing for long periods without winning. Which schedule explains this, and why?
options: continuous: every play is rewarded, so players have no reason to stop playing
fixed ratio: a win comes after a set number of plays, so players count them
variable ratio: a win could come on any play, so play is hard to extinguish
fixed interval: wins come after set times, so players wait for the time to pass
questions.explanation: On a variable-ratio schedule, reinforcement follows an unpredictable number of responses, producing high, steady responding that is very resistant to extinction.

questions.stem: Checking social media for new messages, which arrive at unpredictable times, is reinforced on which schedule?
questions.explanation: On a variable-interval schedule, the first response after an unpredictable amount of time is reinforced. Messages arrive at unpredictable times regardless of how often someone checks.

questions.stem: To teach a child to tie shoelaces, a parent praises first crossing the laces, then making a loop, then the full bow. This is:
questions.explanation: Shaping reinforces successive approximations of the target behaviour, gradually requiring closer matches before reinforcement is given.

questions.stem: In a school program, students earn stickers for completing homework, which they swap for free time at the end of the week. This is:
questions.explanation: A token economy gives tokens (secondary reinforcers) for desired behaviours, which can be exchanged for backup reinforcers. It is an application of operant conditioning.

questions.stem: In Seligman's research, dogs given shocks they could not escape later failed to escape shocks even when escape was easy. This is:
questions.explanation: Learned helplessness occurs when repeated experience of uncontrollable events leads an organism to stop trying, even when it could succeed. Seligman linked it to depression in humans.

questions.stem: Mowrer's two-factor theory explains why a phobia of dogs persists. Which statement matches the theory?
options: Fear is acquired by observation and kept by positive reinforcement from friends and family
Fear is acquired by operant conditioning and kept by classical conditioning through pairing
Fear is acquired by insight learning and kept by latent learning that is not yet shown
Fear is acquired by classical conditioning and kept by negatively reinforced avoidance
questions.explanation: Fear is first learned when the dog is paired with something frightening (classical conditioning). Avoiding dogs then reduces anxiety, and this relief negatively reinforces avoidance, so the fear never has a chance to extinguish.

questions.stem: Which comparison of classical and operant conditioning is correct?
options: In both kinds of conditioning the response must be an involuntary reflex to be learned
In classical conditioning the learner is passive; in operant conditioning the learner is active
In classical conditioning the response is voluntary; in operant conditioning it is reflexive
In classical conditioning the stimulus follows the response; in operant the stimulus comes first
questions.explanation: In classical conditioning, the learner passively responds with a reflexive response to stimuli presented before it. In operant conditioning, the learner actively produces a voluntary behaviour and the consequence follows it.

questions.stem: In operant conditioning, extinction occurs when:
options: an unpleasant stimulus is removed after a response
a similar stimulus produces the same response
the reinforcer no longer follows the behaviour
the CS is presented again without the UCS
questions.explanation: In operant conditioning, a behaviour extinguishes when it stops being reinforced. In classical conditioning, extinction occurs when the CS is repeatedly presented without the UCS.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the processes in Bandura's observational learning?
questions.explanation: The learner must attend to the model, retain a mental representation, be able to reproduce the behaviour, be motivated to do so, and then be reinforced for it.

questions.stem: A Year 7 student watches older students skateboard tricks and remembers them, but cannot yet do them because he lacks the strength and balance. Which process is missing?
questions.explanation: Reproduction requires the physical and mental ability to perform the observed behaviour. He has attended and retained the tricks but cannot yet reproduce them.

questions.stem: A girl sees her older brother praised for cleaning his room and starts cleaning her own room. This is:
questions.explanation: Vicarious reinforcement occurs when observing a model being rewarded increases the likelihood that the observer will perform the behaviour.

questions.stem: A child is more likely to imitate a model who is:
options: punished each time they behave that way
of high status and similar to the child
of low status and unlike the child
a stranger seen only once, briefly
questions.explanation: Models who are admired, powerful, warm or similar to the observer are more likely to be imitated. Seeing a model punished reduces imitation.

questions.stem: Three groups of children watch an adult attack an inflatable doll; for one group the adult is scolded afterwards. That group copies the attack least, until all children are promised treats for copying, when the groups copy equally. This shows:
options: rewards create new learning that did not exist before
children learn only from models who are rewarded
learning can occur without being shown in performance
punishment prevents any learning from taking place
questions.explanation: All the children had learned the behaviour, but those who saw the model punished did not perform it until given an incentive. This distinguishes learning from performance.

questions.stem: Kohler's chimpanzee Sultan, after failing to reach a banana, sat for a while and then suddenly joined two sticks together to reach it. This is:
questions.explanation: Insight learning is the sudden realisation of a solution, often after a period of thinking without obvious progress. It is a mental reorganisation of the problem, not gradual trial and error.

questions.stem: In Tolman's maze studies, rats that explored a maze for ten days without reward made very few errors as soon as food was introduced. This shows:
options: negative reinforcement, because the maze was unpleasant
latent learning, because they had formed a cognitive map
insight learning, because they solved the maze all at once
shaping, because their behaviour was rewarded in small steps
questions.explanation: The rats had learned the layout of the maze (a cognitive map) without reinforcement, but this latent learning only showed once food gave them a reason to perform.

questions.stem: A cognitive map is:
options: a schedule showing when reinforcement will be delivered
a list of feared situations used in desensitisation therapy
a mental representation of the layout of an environment
a diagram drawn to show the stages of operant conditioning
questions.explanation: Tolman proposed that animals and people form internal mental representations of spatial layouts, called cognitive maps, which allow flexible navigation.

questions.stem: After solving many problems of the same type, a student finds each new problem of that type easier to solve. This is the formation of:
questions.explanation: A learning set is the improvement in solving new problems of a type after experience with similar problems, described as learning how to learn.

questions.stem: A tennis player finds that her habit of a firm wrist makes learning a badminton smash harder. This is:
questions.explanation: Negative transfer occurs when previous learning interferes with new learning. Positive transfer occurs when previous learning makes new learning easier.

questions.stem: In Maier's (1931) two-string problem, participants had to tie together two strings hanging too far apart to reach at once. Many solved it after the experimenter brushed against one string. What does this show?
options: A subtle cue can help restructure a problem and trigger insight
Problem solving depends only on reinforcement of correct moves
Participants who solved it had seen a model solve the problem
People solve problems only through repeated trial and error
questions.explanation: Setting the string swinging hinted at the solution of tying a weight to one string and using it as a pendulum. This shows how problem solving depends on cognitive restructuring, an application of cognitive learning.
